title: Cobalt Finance — Security review: Dedicated Burst audit logging + RBAC
summary: Cobalt Finance security team reviewed Redwood’s audit logging and RBAC model for the Dedicated “Burst Capacity” feature. Customer asked for: (1) concrete audit event types for burst config changes and admin overrides, (2) who can make changes (RBAC + SSO/SAML), (3) retention options and export to their SIEM, and (4) evidence that customer admins can independently audit changes vs Redwood Support actions. Redwood explained planned audit events (enable/disable, limit updates, cooldown/ratio changes, tier changes, policy override, emergency circuit breaker), separation of duties (customer admin vs Redwood operator), read vs write permissions, and log export/retention approach (Console + API export, with longer retention for enterprise). Next steps include sharing a sample audit event payload/redacted examples and confirming Cobalt’s retention and SIEM ingestion requirements.
topics: Burst feature scope (Dedicated only) and what constitutes a “burst config change”
Audit event types + fields (who/what/when/where, before/after, reason codes)
RBAC: tenant admins vs Redwood operators; break-glass workflow
Retention and export (Console view, API, SIEM-friendly formats)
Data residency + region scoping of burst pools
Customer questions on circuit breaker actions and transparency
next_steps: Redwood to share draft burst audit events list + sample redacted JSON payloads for Cobalt review.
Cobalt to confirm required audit log retention period and whether they need immutable/WORM storage evidence.
Schedule 30-min follow-up with Cobalt GRC to map controls to SOC 2 / internal policy language.
Redwood to confirm whether audit logs can be exported to customer-owned S3 (or delivered via webhook) at GA for Dedicated Burst.
action_items: Naomi Feldman: Send Cobalt the burst audit events catalog (enable/disable, limit changes, tier changes, override, circuit breaker) and example entries by 2025-04-04.
Marcus Lin: Confirm retention defaults and enterprise retention options for audit logs (Console + export) by 2025-04-04.
Simran Kaur: Provide a one-pager on RBAC roles for Dedicated tenants (read-only support vs tenant admin write) by 2025-04-05.
Ava Patel: Share Cobalt’s SIEM ingestion constraints (format, fields, delivery method, frequency) by 2025-04-08.
Jonah Stein: Confirm compliance requirement for “before/after” values and actor identity (SAML subject vs API key) by 2025-04-08.
transcript:
Meeting header
- Date: 2025-04-02
- Time: 12:05pm–12:57pm ET
- Duration: 52 min
- Call type: Security / compliance review
- Customer: Cobalt Finance
- Redwood: Stephanie Nguyen (AE), Simran Kaur (Solutions Architect), Naomi Feldman (Security/Compliance Product), Marcus Lin (Security Engineering)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
Cobalt asked about audit trails for the new Dedicated Burst option, specifically who can change burst settings, what events are logged, how long logs are retained, and how to export them to their SIEM. Redwood described planned audit events for config changes and admin overrides, RBAC separation, and retention/export options.


Transcript

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool, alright. Thanks everyone for joining. This is the security review focused on the Dedicated burst capacity option, specifically audit logging and access controls. Ava, Jonah, Mina—thanks for making the time.

[00:15] Ava Patel: Yep. Thanks, Stephanie. And just level-set, our main gating items are: audit logs for configuration changes, RBAC, retention period, and the ability to pull those logs into our SIEM. Also, we need clarity on what Redwood Support can do versus what we control.

[00:32] Stephanie Nguyen: Totally. I’ll do quick intros and then hand to Naomi and Marcus.

[00:38] Simran Kaur: Simran, solutions architect.

[00:41] Naomi Feldman: Naomi, security/compliance product review.

[00:44] Marcus Lin: Marcus, security engineering.

[00:47] Mina Kwon: Mina, I’m on platform engineering, I own the deployment side.

[00:52] Jonah Stein: Jonah, GRC/compliance.

[00:55] Ava Patel: Ava, security engineering.

[00:57] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Naomi, do you want to start with how we think about audit logs for burst?

[01:03] Naomi Feldman: Sure. So, dedicated burst capacity is a Dedicated-only feature where you can temporarily exceed your reserved baseline, within limits. From an audit perspective we treat “burst config” like any other tenant configuration that impacts capacity and billing. So we emit audit events whenever those settings change, plus events when Redwood operators do an override or use a break-glass capability.

[01:28] Ava Patel: When you say “emit audit events,” where do they live? Is it just in your console, or is it an API?

[01:35] Marcus Lin: Both. There’s a Console view for human review and an API for export. For certain enterprise packages we also support scheduled export. The exact delivery mechanism—S3 export vs webhook—depends on the deployment mode; for Dedicated, we’re targeting export options that play nicely with SIEM pipelines.

[01:55] Jonah Stein: Before we get into delivery, can we define exactly what actions generate audit events? Like, list them. Because “burst” is new and our control library wants explicit enumerations.

[02:06] Naomi Feldman: Yep. The draft set we’re working with includes:
- Burst enabled / disabled for tenant
- Burst limit updated (e.g., max burst ratio, max burst GPUs, per-tenant cap)
- Priority tier changed (if you’re on a tiered plan)
- Cooldown window changes
- Any policy override applied by Redwood (temporary)
- Override removed / expired
- Emergency circuit breaker actions taken at the fleet level that affect admission
- And also changes to which regions / hardware classes are allow-listed for burst for your tenant

[02:41] Ava Patel: Okay. For the emergency circuit breaker one, is that like Redwood toggles something and suddenly we get denied, and you log it?

[02:49] Marcus Lin: Exactly. There’s a “global safety” mechanism—if enabling burst is causing neighbor SLO impact or fleet saturation, we can clamp down. When that affects a tenant, we want an auditable record. It’s not a tenant config change per se, but it is an administrative action affecting behavior.

[03:08] Mina Kwon: Is that event per-tenant, or just global?

[03:11] Marcus Lin: We have an internal global event, and then a customer-visible derived event for impacted tenants. The customer-visible one is basically: circuit breaker engaged for region/hardware, resulting policy is “burst denied” with a reason.

[03:27] Jonah Stein: What fields do you put in those audit events? We need actor identity, time, what changed, and ideally before/after.

[03:36] Naomi Feldman: Standard fields: timestamp, tenant ID, environment (prod/stage), region, actor type (customer admin vs Redwood operator vs automated system), actor identifier, action name, and the change set. For config updates, we include before/after values. For example: “max_burst_ratio: 1.5 → 2.0” or “burst_enabled: false → true.”

[04:03] Ava Patel: Actor identifier meaning what—SAML user? API key? Support person email?

[04:09] Marcus Lin: Good question. If the change is done via Console with SSO, we log the SAML subject and our internal user ID, plus email if present. If it’s via API, we log the API credential identifier—like key ID—and if it’s OAuth we log the client ID. For Redwood operators, we log the Redwood user ID plus the on-call role used, and there’s an explicit “break-glass” flag when that path is used.

[04:36] Ava Patel: We’ll need to see that in an example because vendors sometimes say “we log it” but it’s like “support-user-1.”

[04:42] Marcus Lin: Totally fair. We can share a redacted sample payload showing the exact fields and what’s stable.

[04:50] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll send that after.

[04:52] Jonah Stein: Is there a “reason” field? Like, why did someone change it, ticket reference, approval, etc.

[05:00] Naomi Feldman: Yes, we have a “reason” and “reference” concept. For customer-initiated changes, it can be optional or required depending on policy. For Redwood-operator actions it’s required and we attach an internal ticket ID (like an INT- ticket) and the approval group.

[05:20] Mina Kwon: Is it possible to require it for our admins? We have a change management policy.

[05:25] Marcus Lin: We can enforce that via RBAC policy in some tenants—like “change requires justification.” I don’t want to over-promise; but we can at least support a “reason” string and you can enforce your own workflow. We can also recommend doing changes through API with your internal system so you can tie it to your change ticket.

[05:48] Ava Patel: Let’s talk RBAC. Who in our org can do what? And what can Redwood Support do?

[05:55] Naomi Feldman: RBAC is role-based, tied to your org in Redwood. At a high level:
- Tenant Admin: can enable/disable burst, change limits, change priorities, and view audit logs
- Tenant Operator: can view settings and audit logs, but cannot change burst policy
- Billing Admin (optional role): can view usage/burst metering reports, not change policy
- Support Viewer (Redwood-side): can view relevant status for debugging, but cannot change tenant config
- Support Operator / On-call (Redwood-side): can change config only via an elevated workflow, which is audited and requires explicit break-glass justification

[06:35] Ava Patel: When you say “cannot change,” is that technically enforced or just policy?

[06:40] Marcus Lin: It’s technically enforced in the control plane service. Support tooling uses separate credentials with scoped permissions. The elevated path uses a separate role with approvals and is also logged.

[06:54] Jonah Stein: Do you have SSO / SAML for this? Because we don’t want local accounts.

[06:59] Naomi Feldman: Yes, for enterprise. SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning. You can disable password auth and require SSO.

[07:10] Mina Kwon: And can we limit to specific groups? Like only infra admins can change burst limits.

[07:16] Marcus Lin: Yes. You map IdP groups to Redwood roles. Tenant Admin is a role; you can keep it very small.

[07:26] Ava Patel: On retention: what’s your default retention for audit logs and can we extend it to a year? Our policy is 365 days online, seven years archive.

[07:36] Naomi Feldman: Default is shorter—think 90 days in Console for standard. For enterprise compliance packages we can retain longer, typically 1 year searchable in Console. For longer-term retention like seven years, we usually recommend export to your storage/SIEM where you control lifecycle.

[08:02] Jonah Stein: Is that export continuous or batch? And format?

[08:06] Marcus Lin: Today for many audit event streams we support batch export (daily) and API pull. We’re aligning burst audit events with the same pipeline. Format is JSON lines (one event per line) or a structured schema via API. If your SIEM prefers syslog, we can discuss via an integration layer, but JSON is the native.

[08:30] Ava Patel: We use Splunk and sometimes we want HEC. Are you doing HEC?

[08:35] Marcus Lin: Not native HEC. Most customers either pull via API and forward, or we deliver to S3/GCS and then they ingest. If HEC is a hard requirement we need to capture that and see if we can support via webhook or partner.

[08:55] Stephanie Nguyen: We can treat it as a requirement and get you an answer rather than guessing.

[09:00] Jonah Stein: For “before and after,” is it full config blob or only changed fields? Our auditors prefer delta, but sometimes also want full state for reconstruction.

[09:11] Naomi Feldman: We log the delta, plus a “config_version” and an optional snapshot pointer. In practice you can reconstruct from deltas if you have the baseline. We can provide full snapshots on request but we try to avoid dumping huge objects in every event.

[09:31] Ava Patel: Okay. How do you handle “burst admission” decisions? Are those audited? Like, if we were denied, is that in audit logs or just metrics?

[09:41] Marcus Lin: Great distinction. Admission decisions happen at request time and can be very high volume. We don’t put every deny into audit logs. We expose denial reason codes via metrics and customer-facing reporting—like “denied due to cap” or “denied due to cooldown.” Audit logs are for administrative/config changes and overrides.

[10:05] Mina Kwon: But if a Redwood operator changes a policy that results in denial, that’s auditable.

[10:10] Marcus Lin: Correct.

[10:12] Jonah Stein: Can you enumerate denial reason codes anyway? That’s more operational, but it helps our incident review.

[10:19] Simran Kaur: We can share the list we publish in docs. Typical ones are like: BURST_DISABLED, TENANT_CAP_REACHED, POOL_SATURATED, COOLDOWN_ACTIVE, FLEET_SAFETY_CAP, TELEMETRY_STALE, and sometimes ROUTING_POLICY.

[10:41] Ava Patel: TELEMETRY_STALE? That sounds scary.

[10:44] Marcus Lin: It’s basically a safety behavior. If the system can’t confidently determine pool headroom due to telemetry lag, it can deny burst rather than risk neighbor impact. It’s conservative. And it’s visible as a reason code.

[11:02] Ava Patel: Is that configurable? Like we can opt out?

[11:05] Marcus Lin: No, that’s part of the platform safety. You can set your baseline capacity so you’re not relying on burst for steady-state.

[11:15] Jonah Stein: Let’s go back to “Redwood operator override.” What is the scenario? Why would Redwood need to change our burst config at all?

[11:24] Naomi Feldman: Usually we don’t. Typical reasons are: you request a change and want us to apply it (during onboarding), or there’s an emergency mitigation where we need to temporarily lower burst caps to protect the fleet and then revert. Another case is correcting a misconfiguration with your approval.

[11:46] Ava Patel: For the emergency mitigation, is that per-tenant? Or do you just flip the global breaker.

[11:51] Marcus Lin: It can be either. Global breaker is preferred because it’s consistent and doesn’t single out. But there are cases where one tenant is bursting in a way that causes localized contention—then we may reduce that tenant’s burst cap. That action is audited with actor and reason, and ideally communicated to you.

[12:16] Mina Kwon: Communication is key. We had an incident with another vendor where they throttled and we found out after.

[12:22] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood. Part of the launch includes customer-visible reporting and Support playbooks so we can explain exactly what happened.

[12:31] Jonah Stein: Do audit logs show IP address or source of the request?

[12:36] Marcus Lin: For API-based changes, yes, we log source IP and user agent when available. For Console, we log session metadata. There are some privacy constraints, but for admin actions we keep enough to support investigations.

[12:55] Ava Patel: Data residency. If bursting is limited to region, are audit logs also region-scoped? We’re US-only.

[13:03] Marcus Lin: Audit logs are part of control plane. We can ensure your tenant data and logs are stored in US regions depending on the plan. For Dedicated, we typically align control plane region to your deployment region. I don’t want to claim “always” without checking your target architecture; but if US-only is a requirement, we’ll capture it and confirm.

[13:29] Jonah Stein: We will need that in writing.

[13:31] Naomi Feldman: Yep.

[13:33] Ava Patel: Another thing: immutability. Can you delete or edit audit events?

[13:38] Marcus Lin: Customers can’t. Redwood operators also can’t modify historical events. It’s append-only in our audit pipeline. There are retention policies where events expire after the retention window, but not selective deletion. For your seven-year requirement, export is the better control, because you can put it into WORM storage if needed.

[14:05] Jonah Stein: Okay. Is there a “view audit logs” permission separate from “change burst config”? We prefer separation.

[14:12] Marcus Lin: Yes. View is separate. You can have read-only auditors.

[14:18] Mina Kwon: Is the audit log accessible via API so we can feed it to our internal GRC tool?

[14:23] Marcus Lin: Yes, we have endpoints for audit events with filters by time range, event type, actor, and so on.

[14:33] Ava Patel: Do you support pagination and stable ordering? Sorry, boring, but SIEM ingestion breaks without it.

[14:39] Marcus Lin: Yes. Cursor-based pagination, stable ordering by timestamp and event ID. We can share details.

[14:50] Simran Kaur: And if you do export, it’s also ordered in the files by timestamp.

[14:55] Jonah Stein: Cooldown windows. You mentioned audit events for cooldown changes. Can customers change cooldown, or is that Redwood-set?

[15:04] Naomi Feldman: For GA, customers can set some parameters within a safe range, depending on packaging. Some guardrails are platform-defined. If cooldown is customer-configurable for your tier, changes are audited.

[15:21] Ava Patel: Do you log policy evaluation changes? Like if Redwood updates the underlying rules engine.

[15:27] Marcus Lin: We log “policy version” associated with admission behavior, but that’s not per-tenant audit unless it changes your effective policy. For example, if we change a global safety threshold, we’d log a global change and it could show up in the “circuit breaker engaged” events if it triggers. For compliance, we can provide release notes and change management evidence.

[15:55] Jonah Stein: We will need release notes anyway, yes.

[15:58] Stephanie Nguyen: We can include that in our security package.

[16:02] Ava Patel: Let’s talk about “burst usage” itself. Is there an audit event when we exceed baseline? That might matter for our internal cost approvals.

[16:12] Naomi Feldman: That’s more metering/reporting than audit log. We provide usage reports—burst GPU-seconds or tokens attributed to burst—depending on how billing is done. It’s not in audit logs because of volume. But it is visible in the Console and exportable.

[16:33] Mina Kwon: For cost, we’d probably want a daily export anyway.

[16:36] Simran Kaur: Yep, and alerts: like “you’re at 80% of burst cap.”

[16:42] Ava Patel: Back to RBAC: Can Redwood Support view our prompts or payloads? This is tangential but related to debugging.

[16:49] Naomi Feldman: By default, for Dedicated we minimize access. Payload logging can be disabled or limited. For burst specifically, Support doesn’t need to see prompts—mostly config and metrics.

[17:05] Marcus Lin: And any Support access is audited on the access log side too, separate from burst audit events.

[17:14] Jonah Stein: Okay. So to be clear, there are two streams: access logs and config audit logs.

[17:20] Marcus Lin: Correct.

[17:22] Ava Patel: Can we get the list of event names with exact spelling? Like “burst.limit.updated” vs “BurstLimitChange.”

[17:29] Marcus Lin: Yes, we’ll send the catalog. Names are snake_case internally but we can present them as a stable schema. Something like:
- dedicated_burst.enabled
- dedicated_burst.disabled
- dedicated_burst.limits.updated
- dedicated_burst.priority_tier.updated
- dedicated_burst.override.applied
- dedicated_burst.override.removed
- dedicated_burst.circuit_breaker.engaged
- dedicated_burst.circuit_breaker.released

[18:04] Ava Patel: Great. Also, do events include the “region/hardware class”? We have multiple hardware types sometimes.

[18:11] Marcus Lin: Yes. Region, hardware class, and the scope—tenant-wide vs per region.

[18:18] Mina Kwon: Scope matters because we might only enable burst on H100 in us-east.

[18:23] Naomi Feldman: Exactly.

[18:25] Jonah Stein: Any concerns on label cardinality? Sorry, I saw a vendor once and their audit logs were missing because they capped fields.

[18:33] Marcus Lin: For audit logs we don’t have the same cardinality issue as metrics, but we still keep the schema bounded. IDs are present, but we avoid arbitrary payload blobs.

[18:48] Ava Patel: Who can view the audit log in Console? Is it visible to all users?

[18:53] Naomi Feldman: No, permissioned. You can restrict to Tenant Admin and Auditor roles.

[19:00] Jonah Stein: Is there alerting on config changes? Like, if someone enables burst, can we get an email?

[19:07] Simran Kaur: We have webhooks for certain events and can integrate with your alerting. If you export to SIEM you can trigger there. Email notifications are on the roadmap but not guaranteed for day one.

[19:23] Ava Patel: We can do SIEM triggers, that’s fine.

[19:26] Stephanie Nguyen: Erik from procurement might join—just FYI.

[19:30] Ava Patel: Cool.

[19:32] Jonah Stein: One more: do audit logs capture failed attempts? Like unauthorized change attempts.

[19:38] Marcus Lin: Yes, we log denied administrative actions—like permission denied events—at least in the security audit stream. For burst config, an unauthorized attempt to change it will be a “policy denied” event including actor and requested action.

[20:00] Ava Patel: That’s important. Thanks.

[20:03] Mina Kwon: If someone tries via API key that’s expired, is that included?

[20:07] Marcus Lin: We log auth failures and authorization failures. The level of detail depends on the error type.

[20:18] Jonah Stein: Great.

[20:21] (cross talk)

[20:22] Stephanie Nguyen: Ava, Jonah—anything else on the audit side? We can also talk about contract language but I think this call is mostly security technical.

[20:32] Ava Patel: I have a question about “Support debug endpoint.” Do you have a tool that explains why a burst was denied? If Support uses it, is that logged?

[20:41] Marcus Lin: Yes, there’s internal tooling to explain admission decisions with redaction. Access to that tool is controlled and audited. It doesn’t expose prompts; it shows config, limits, and reason codes.

[20:56] Ava Patel: Good.

[20:58] Jonah Stein: Retention again: you said 90 days default and 1 year for enterprise. Is the 1 year guaranteed contractually?

[21:06] Naomi Feldman: Typically yes, in the security addendum or order form if it’s a requirement. We’ll coordinate with legal on the specific language.

[21:18] Jonah Stein: Okay.

[21:20] Erik Lund: Hey, sorry, I joined late. Erik from procurement. I’m mostly listening.

[21:24] Stephanie Nguyen: Hey Erik.

[21:26] Erik Lund: Quick question, does audit log export cost extra?

[21:31] Stephanie Nguyen: It can depend on the package. We can follow up with a pricing breakdown. Today we’re focusing on what’s technically supported.

[21:41] Erik Lund: Got it.

[21:44] Ava Patel: One edge case: can Redwood change our burst config without our consent?

[21:50] Naomi Feldman: Only in limited operational circumstances, like incident mitigation. It’s audited, and we aim to notify you. For general changes, no—we require your request/approval.

[22:04] Ava Patel: We’ll want that spelled out.

[22:07] Stephanie Nguyen: We can loop in legal and put it in the addendum.

[22:12] Jonah Stein: How do you handle time sync? Audit logs need reliable timestamps.

[22:17] Marcus Lin: Events are stamped by our control plane using synchronized time sources; we also include received_at and processed_at. It’s standard for our audit pipeline.

[22:32] Mina Kwon: Do you include request IDs? So we can correlate.

[22:36] Marcus Lin: Yes—request ID / trace ID for API changes.

[22:42] Ava Patel: Okay. I think what we need from you is: a sample audit event, the schema, retention commitments, export options, and RBAC role matrix.

[22:55] Naomi Feldman: Yep.

[22:57] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s do a quick recap of what we’ll send.

[23:01] Stephanie Nguyen: Naomi will send the burst audit events catalog and sample payloads, Marcus will confirm retention and export mechanism options, Simran will send the RBAC mapping one-pager.

[23:16] Ava Patel: Works.

[23:18] Jonah Stein: And we’ll get back with SIEM constraints and whether we need WORM/immutability attestation.

[23:25] Marcus Lin: Perfect.

[23:28] (short pause)

[23:30] Mina Kwon: One last quick technical: Are audit logs available in a Private deployment too? Like if we go VPC later.

[23:36] Marcus Lin: Yes, but the storage/export patterns can differ. For Dedicated hosted control plane, Redwood hosts the audit pipeline. For VPC/private, we can deploy components into your environment. But for this deal, we’re talking Dedicated.

[23:55] Mina Kwon: Got it.

[23:57] Ava Patel: Alright, thanks. This was helpful.

[24:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. We’ll send the follow-ups by end of week. Anything else before we drop?

[24:08] Erik Lund: Nothing from me.

[24:10] Jonah Stein: Good.

[24:12] Ava Patel: Thanks.

[24:14] Stephanie Nguyen: Thanks everyone.

Note: Fireflies transcript ended early at ~24 min due to recording permissions; remaining discussion (~28 min) continued without recording and covered: Splunk HEC vs S3 export options, and whether “change justification required” could be enforced for customer admins. Redwood agreed to confirm feasibility and provide written guidance.
